# Installing django

Installing `django` from the `conda-forge` channel can be achieved by adding `conda-forge` to your channels with:

```
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict
```
Once the `conda-forge` channel has been enabled, `django` can be installed with `conda` :

```
conda install django
```

or with `mamba` :

```
mamba install django
```

It is possible to list all of the versions of `django` available on your platform with `conda` :

```
conda search django --channel conda-forge
```

or with `mamba` :

```
mamba search django --channel conda-forge
```

Alternatively, `mamba repoquery` may provide more information:

```
# Search all versions available on your platform:
mamba repoquery search django --channel conda-forge

# List packages depending on `django`:
mamba repoquery whoneeds django --channel conda-forge

# List dependencies of `django`:
mamba repoquery depends django --channel conda-forge
```

# About conda-forge

[Powered by NumFOCUS](https://numfocus.org)

conda-forge is a community-led conda channel of installable packages.
In order to provide high-quality builds, the process has been automated into the
conda-forge GitHub organization.
The conda-forge organization contains one repository
for each of the installable packages. Such a repository is known as a _feedstock_ .

A feedstock is made up of a conda recipe (the instructions on what and how to build
the package) and the necessary configurations for automatic building using freely
available continuous integration services. Thanks to the awesome service provided by [Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/devops/) , [GitHub](https://github.com/) , [CircleCI](https://circleci.com/) , [AppVeyor](https://www.appveyor.com/) , [Drone](https://cloud.drone.io/welcome) , and [TravisCI](https://travis-ci.com/) it is possible to build and upload installable packages to the [conda-forge](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge) [anaconda.org](https://anaconda.org/) channel for Linux, Windows and OSX respectively.

To manage the continuous integration and simplify feedstock maintenance [conda-smithy](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-smithy) has been developed.
Using the `conda-forge.yml` within this repository, it is possible to re-render all of
this feedstock's supporting files (e.g. the CI configuration files) with `conda smithy rerender` .

For more information please check the [conda-forge documentation](https://conda-forge.org/docs/) .

# Terminology

**feedstock** \- the conda recipe (raw material), supporting scripts and CI configuration.

**conda-smithy** \- the tool which helps orchestrate the feedstock.
Its primary use is in the construction of the CI `.yml` files
and simplify the management of _many_ feedstocks.

**conda-forge** \- the place where the feedstock and smithy live and work to
produce the finished article (built conda distributions)

# Updating django-feedstock

If you would like to improve the django recipe or build a new
package version, please fork this repository and submit a PR. Upon submission,
your changes will be run on the appropriate platforms to give the reviewer an
opportunity to confirm that the changes result in a successful build. Once
merged, the recipe will be re-built and uploaded automatically to the `conda-forge` channel, whereupon the built conda packages will be available for
everybody to install and use from the `conda-forge` channel.
Note that all branches in the conda-forge/django-feedstock are
immediately built and any created packages are uploaded, so PRs should be based
on branches in forks and branches in the main repository should only be used to
build distinct package versions.

In order to produce a uniquely identifiable distribution:

* If the version of a package **is not** being increased, please add or increase
  the [`build/number`](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda-build/en/latest/resources/define-metadata.html) .
* If the version of a package **is** being increased, please remember to return
  the [`build/number`](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda-build/en/latest/resources/define-metadata.html) back to 0.

The short answer is that, in my experience generally, it doesn't matter which you use, with one exception. If you work for a company with more than 200 employees then the `default` conda channel is [not free as of 2020.](https://www.anaconda.com/blog/is-conda-free)

The long answer:

So `conda-forge` is an additional channel from which packages may be installed. In this sense, it is not any more special than the default channel, or any of the other hundreds (thousands?) of channels that people have posted packages to. You can add your own channel if you sign up at <https://anaconda.
org> and upload your own Conda packages.

Here we need to make the distinction, which I think you're not clear about from your phrasing in the question, between `conda` , the cross-platform package manager, and `conda-forge` , the package channel. Anaconda Inc. (formerly Continuum IO), the main developers of the `conda` software, also maintain a separate channel of packages, which is the default when you type `conda install packagename` without changing any options.

There are three ways to change the options for channels. The first two are done every time you install a package and the last one is persistent. The first one is to specify a channel every time you install a package:

```
conda install -c some-channel packagename
```

Of course, the package has to exist on that channel. This way will install `packagename` and all its dependencies from `some-channel` . Alternately, you can specify:

```
conda install some-channel::packagename
```
The package still has to exist on `some-channel` , but now, only `packagename` will be pulled from `some-channel` . Any other packages that are needed to satisfy dependencies will be searched for from your default list of channels.

To see your channel configuration, you can write:

```
conda config --show channels
```

You can control the order that channels are searched with `conda config` . You can write:

```
conda config --add channels some-channel
```

to add the channel `some-channel` to the top of the `channels` configuration list. This gives `some-channel` the highest priority. Priority determines ( [in part](http://conda.pydata.org/docs/channels.html) ) which channel is selected when more than one channel has a particular package. To add the channel to the end of the list and give it the lowest priority, type

```
conda config --append channels some-channel
```

If you would like to remove the channel that you added, you can do so by writing

```
conda config --remove channels some-channel
```

See

```
conda config -h
```

for more options.

With all of that said, there are five main reasons to use the `conda-forge` channel instead of the `defaults` channel maintained by Anaconda:

1. Packages on `conda-forge` _may_ be more up-to-date than those on the `defaults` channel
2. There are packages on the `conda-forge` channel that aren't available from `defaults`
3. You would prefer to use a dependency such as `openblas` (from `conda-forge` ) instead of `mkl` (from `defaults` ).
4. If you are installing a package that requires a compiled library (e.g., a C extension or a wrapper around a C library), it _may_ reduce the chance of incompatibilities if you install all of the packages in an environment from a single channel due to binary compatibility of the base C library (but this advice may be out of date/change in the future). For reference, see [the Conda Forge post on mixing channels](https://conda-forge.
org/docs/user/tipsandtricks.html) .
5. conda-forge is free to use even in large companies, while the default conda channel is not. [See here.](https://www.anaconda.com/blog/is-conda-free)

Anaconda has changed their [Terms of Service](https://www.anaconda.com/blog/sustaining-our-stewardship-of-the-open-source-data-science-community) so that "heavy commercial users" would have to pay, which doesn't include `conda-forge` channel. That includes most organisations, including research organisations who are over 200 people.

The `main` channel is maintained by Anaconda, while `conda-forge` is maintained by the maintainers of the packages themselves. Each have their pros and cons.
Packages on the `main` channel are usually compatible with one another, meaning you can install almost as many as you want, and you won't have dependency conflicts. On the other hand, packages on the `conda-forge` channel receive the updates much faster than the `main` channel since the maintainers themselves push the updates to the channel. From time to time, there are also patches done by Anaconda on packages available on the `main` channel which are not supported and done by the maintainers of the package, which can be good or bad, but definitely out of hands of the maintainers and not supported by them.

You probably would want to stick to `conda-forge` if you don't want to pay for the usage and you would be okay with the versions available on [`pypi`](https://pypi.org/) . As stated in the [docs](https://conda-forge.org/) :

```
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict
conda install <package-name>
```
You could also use [miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/) which has `conda-forge` as the default channel, and supports ppc64le and aarch64 platforms as well as the other usual ones.

If you have `conda` installed and would like to remove the default channels, you can use

```
conda config --show channels
```

to see your channels, and can use

```
conda config --remove channels channel-name
```

to remove a channel.

# Installing pillow

Installing `pillow` from the `conda-forge` channel can be achieved by adding `conda-forge` to your channels with:

```
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict
```

Once the `conda-forge` channel has been enabled, `pillow, pillow-tests` can be installed with `conda` :

```
conda install pillow pillow-tests
```

or with `mamba` :

```
mamba install pillow pillow-tests
```

It is possible to list all of the versions of `pillow` available on your platform with `conda` :

```
conda search pillow --channel conda-forge
```

or with `mamba` :

```
mamba search pillow --channel conda-forge
```

Alternatively, `mamba repoquery` may provide more information:

```
# Search all versions available on your platform:
mamba repoquery search pillow --channel conda-forge

# List packages depending on `pillow`:
mamba repoquery whoneeds pillow --channel conda-forge

# List dependencies of `pillow`:
mamba repoquery depends pillow --channel conda-forge
```

conda-forge is a community-led conda channel of installable packages.
In order to provide high-quality builds, the process has been automated into the
conda-forge GitHub organization. The conda-forge organization contains one repository
for each of the installable packages. Such a repository is known as a _feedstock_ .

A feedstock is made up of a conda recipe (the instructions on what and how to build
the package) and the necessary configurations for automatic building using freely
available continuous integration services.

...

**feedstock** \- the conda recipe (raw material), supporting scripts and CI configuration.

**conda-smithy** \- the tool which helps orchestrate the feedstock.
Its primary use is in the construction of the CI `.yml` files
and simplify the management of _many_ feedstocks.

**conda-forge** \- the place where the feedstock and smithy live and work to
produce the finished article (built conda distributions)

package version, please fork this repository and submit a PR. Upon submission,
your changes will be run on the appropriate platforms to give the reviewer an
opportunity to confirm that the changes result in a successful build. Once

everybody to install and use from the `conda-forge` channel.

immediately built and any created packages are uploaded, so PRs should be based

text:
Here's the comparison:

---

## 1. Django (5.0.11) + ecosystem (DRF, allauth, crispy, etc.)

| Factor | pip | conda-forge |
|---|---|---|
| **Django version available** | 5.2.x latest | 5.0.11 (pinned here), 6.0.7 also available |
| **Extra complexity** | many `django-*` packages resolve independently | conda's SAT solver reconciles all Django ecosystem packages together |

**Conflict reality:** The project pins `django<5.1`. With pip, this constraint is advisory — `pip install` happily resolves `django-allauth==65.3.1` against `django==5.0.11` with no issues since none of the Django packages here have tight upper bounds. With conda, the SAT solver also resolves fine because all `django-*` packages on conda-forge are `noarch` with flexible deps. **Neither handles conflicts better here** — both resolve identically for this stack.

**Edge case where conda wins:** If `django-crispy-forms` bumped to requiring `django>=5.1`, pip would happily install it alongside your pinned `django==5.0.11` at install time (only breaking at runtime). Conda's solver would detect the constraint violation and refuse to solve. Ties in conda's favor for **install-time vs runtime failure**.

---

## 2. psycopg2 (2.9.10) / psycopg (v3)

| Factor | pip | conda-forge |
|---|---|---|
| **psycopg2-binary** | 2.9.10 | ✅ available (same version) |
| **psycopg (v3)** | `psycopg[c]==3.2.x` | ❌ **NOT on conda-forge** (missing entirely) |
| **C library linkage** | compiled at install / wheel | pre-linked against conda's `libpq` |

**Conflict reality:** The project uses `psycopg2==2.9.10` (old ABI) with `psycopg2-binary` also pinned in the freeze. The commented-out `# psycopg[c]==3.2.4` in `production.txt` signals intent to migrate to v3 but it's blocked — likely because `psycopg` v3 is **not on conda-forge at all**. This is a real problem: switching to psycopg v3 would force pip-only for that single dependency, creating a split environment.

**Verdict:** pip wins here — `psycopg` v3 is only available on PyPI, and since this project is considering migrating to it, pip gives you the option while conda doesn't. For the current `psycopg2` setup, conda's `libpq` linkage is more robust (avoids macOS Homebrew `libpq` version mismatches), but the migration path favors pip.

---

## 3. mypy + django-stubs + django-stubs-ext

| Factor | pip | conda-forge |
|---|---|---|
| **mypy** | `1.13.0` | ✅ `1.13.0` available |
| **django-stubs** | `5.1.2` | ✅ available |
| **djangorestframework-stubs** | `3.15.2` | ✅ available |
| **Version coupling** | MyPy 1.13 ↔ django-stubs 5.1.2 ↔ Django 5.0.x tightly linked | same tight coupling |
| **typing_extensions** | `4.12.2` | ✅ available |

**Conflict reality:** This is the most conflict-sensitive ecosystem in the project. `django-stubs` releases track Django minor versions: `django-stubs 5.1.x` matches `Django 5.1.x`, `5.0.x` matches `Django 5.0.x`. If pip upgrades Django to 5.1 without also upgrading `django-stubs`, mypy breaks. Pip's resolver handles this fine as long as all pins are explicit.

**The real conda win:** Conda's SAT solver can express `django-stubs>=5.0,<5.1` naturally if the feedstock metadata is correct. With pip, this relies entirely on the user maintaining correct upper bounds in `requirements/*.txt`. The `# pyup: < 5.1` comment on Django shows the project is already doing this manually for pip. Conda would enforce it automatically through the solver if the feedstock dependency metadata is accurate — but conda-forge feedstocks occasionally lag the actual package metadata, meaning the solver can also give **false negatives** (failing to resolve when it should work).

**Verdict:** Slight edge to conda for automated constraint enforcement, but in practice both work identically because the project already pins aggressively.

---

## Bottom Line

| Group | Better solver | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Django + DRF + allauth | **Conda** (marginal) | Install-time vs runtime failure detection for unexpected upper-bound bumps |
| psycopg2 / psycopg v3 | **Pip** | `psycopg` v3 doesn't exist on conda-forge — migration path is pip-only |
| mypy + django-stubs | **Tie** | Both resolve identically; conda's SAT has theoretical edge but feedstocks lag |

**Cross-cutting issue not specific to these three:** The project pins exact versions everywhere (`==`), which largely neutralizes conda's SAT advantage. Conda's solver excels with loose constraints (`>=`); with strict pins, pip's resolver behaves identically. The project's manual upper-bound comments (`# pyup: < 5.1`) are a pip-native version of what conda's solver would do automatically.

---

## Requirements Files Available

| File | Path |
|---|---|
| **base.txt** | `/Users/dk/lab-data/oleovista-acers/acers-backend/acers/requirements/base.txt` |

The `requirements/` directory is copied wholesale (`COPY ./requirements .` or `COPY ./requirements /requirements`) into the Docker build context so the Dockerfiles can reference files by their basename.

---

## 1. `compose/local/django/Dockerfile` (used by `docker-compose.local.yml`)

**Build stage** -- wheels are built from the requirements file matching the `BUILD_ENVIRONMENT` arg (defaults to `local`):

```dockerfile
ARG BUILD_ENVIRONMENT=local
COPY ./requirements .
RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /usr/src/app/wheels \
  -r ${BUILD_ENVIRONMENT}.txt
```

This resolves to **`-r local.txt`** (a full UTF-16 LE pip-freeze-style file with all dependencies pinned -- it does NOT `-r base.txt`; it's a standalone frozen list).

**Run stage** -- installs from the pre-built wheels (no network, no index):

```dockerfile
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels/ /wheels/* \
  && rm -rf /wheels/
```

---

## 2. `compose/production/django/Dockerfile` (used by `docker-compose.production.yml`)

Identical pattern, but `BUILD_ENVIRONMENT` defaults to `production`:

**Build stage:**
```dockerfile
ARG BUILD_ENVIRONMENT=production
COPY ./requirements .
RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /usr/src/app/wheels \
  -r ${BUILD_ENVIRONMENT}.txt
```

This resolves to **`-r production.txt`**.

`production.txt` is a lightweight file that **`-r base.txt`** first, then adds production-specific packages:
```
-r base.txt

gunicorn==23.0.0
sentry-sdk==2.20.0
django-storages[azure]==1.14.4
django-anymail==12.0
```

**Run stage** -- same wheel-install pattern:
```dockerfile
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels/ /wheels/* \
  && rm -rf /wheels/
```

---

## 3. `compose/local/docs/Dockerfile` (used by `docker-compose.docs.yml`)

The docs image breaks the pattern -- it installs **both** `local.txt` **and** `production.txt` wheels in one build stage:

**Build stage:**
```dockerfile
COPY ./requirements /requirements
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /usr/src/app/wheels \
  -r /requirements/local.txt -r /requirements/production.txt \
  && rm -rf /requirements
```

**Run stage** -- simpler install (no `--no-index`/`--find-links`, just direct wheel install):
```dockerfile
RUN pip install --no-cache /wheels/* \
  && rm -rf /wheels
```

---

## 4. No root-level Dockerfile

There is **no** `Dockerfile` at the repository root. All Dockerfiles live under `compose/`.

---

## Summary Table

| Compose file | Dockerfile | Requirements file(s) used | pip install method |
|---|---|---|---|
| `docker-compose.local.yml` | `compose/local/django/Dockerfile` | `local.txt` (full freeze) | Two-stage: `pip wheel` then `pip install --no-index --find-links=/wheels/` |
| `docker-compose.production.yml` | `compose/production/django/Dockerfile` | `production.txt` (includes `base.txt` via `-r`) | Two-stage: `pip wheel` then `pip install --no-index --find-links=/wheels/` |
| `docker-compose.docs.yml` | `compose/local/docs/Dockerfile` | `local.txt` + `production.txt` (both) | Two-stage: `pip wheel` then `pip install --no-cache /wheels/*` |

**Key design pattern**: All three Django Dockerfiles use a two-stage Docker build (wheel-build stage + run stage). Requirements are resolved into wheels in the first stage, and the run stage installs those wheels offline -- avoiding network calls and repeated dependency resolution during the run stage. The `BUILD_ENVIRONMENT` arg (`local` or `production`) determines which `requirements/<env>.txt` file is used to build the wheels.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
SSOT-backed requirements export — regenerate requirements/*.txt from environment.yml.

Usage:
    python scripts/export_requirements.py        # write all three
    python scripts/export_requirements.py --check # verify SSOT is up to date
"""

import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
ENV_YML = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "environment.yml")
REQS_DIR = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "requirements")

# Which environment.yml section headers map to which requirements file.
# "prod" → base.txt + production.txt, "dev" → local.txt only, "prod-only" → production.txt only.
SECTION_CLASSIFICATION = {
    "Web Framework":                    "prod",
    "ASGI / WebSockets":               "prod",
    "Authentication & Security":        "prod",
    "Database & Storage":               "prod",
    "Task Queue":                       "prod",
    "HTTP & Networking":                "prod",
    "Static Assets / Media":            "prod",
    "Data Processing":                  "prod",
    "Payment / API":                    "prod",
    "Templating / Markup":              "prod",
    "Testing & QA":                     "dev",
    "Dev Tooling":                      "dev",
    "Pre-commit Transitives":           "dev",
}

# Packages that should appear only in production.txt (not base.txt), keeping
# the existing convention. These are typically infra-level concerns.
PROD_ONLY = {"gunicorn", "sentry-sdk", "django-storages", "django-anymail"}


def parse_environment_yml(path):
    """Return (conda_deps, pip_deps) where each is a list of (name, version, section)."""
    conda = []
    pip = []
    current_section = None

    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            stripped = line.strip()

            section_match = re.match(r"# ── (.+?) ──", stripped)
            if section_match:
                current_section = section_match.group(1)
                continue

            if stripped.startswith("- pip:"):
                continue  # pip block header
            if current_section == "PyPI-only (fallback via pip)":
                if stripped.startswith("- ") and "==" in stripped:
                    name, ver = stripped[2:].split("==", 1)
                    pip.append((name.strip(), ver.strip(), current_section))
                continue

            if stripped.startswith("- ") and "=" in stripped and "==" not in stripped:
                # conda-style: - pkg=1.0
                entry = stripped[2:]
                if entry.startswith("pip"):
                    continue
                name, ver = entry.split("=", 1)
                conda.append((name.strip(), ver.strip(), current_section))

    return conda, pip


def format_pip_line(name, version, section):
    comment = f"  # {section}" if section else ""
    return f"{name}=={version}{comment}"


def write_requirements(packages, pip_deps, path, header_lines=None, include_line=None):
    lines = []
    if header_lines:
        lines.extend(header_lines)
    if include_line:
        lines.append(include_line)
        lines.append("")

    by_section = {}
    for pkg in packages:
        s = pkg[2] or "Other"
        by_section.setdefault(s, []).append(pkg)

    for section in sorted(by_section.keys()):
        sec_label = section.replace("_", " ").title()
        env_type = SECTION_CLASSIFICATION.get(section, "dev")
        lines.append(f"# ── {sec_label} ────────────────────────────────────────────")
        for name, ver, _ in sorted(by_section[section], key=lambda x: x[0].lower()):
            lines.append(format_pip_line(name, ver, section))
        lines.append("")

    # Append pip-only deps at the end

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
SSOT-backed requirements export — regenerate requirements/*.txt from environment.yml.

Usage:
    python scripts/export_requirements.py        # write all three
    python scripts/export_requirements.py --check # verify SSOT is up to date
"""

import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
ENV_YML = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "environment.yml")
REQS_DIR = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "requirements")

# Which environment.yml section headers map to which requirements file.
# "prod" → base.txt + production.txt, "dev" → local.txt only, "prod-only" → production.txt only.
SECTION_CLASSIFICATION = {
    "Web Framework":                    "prod",
    "ASGI / WebSockets":               "prod",
    "Authentication & Security":        "prod",
    "Database & Storage":               "prod",
    "Task Queue":                       "prod",
    "HTTP & Networking":                "prod",
    "Static Assets / Media":            "prod",
    "Data Processing":                  "prod",
    "Payment / API":                    "prod",
    "Templating / Markup":              "prod",
    "Testing & QA":                     "dev",
    "Dev Tooling":                      "dev",
    "Pre-commit Transitives":           "dev",
}

# Packages that should appear only in production.txt (not base.txt), keeping
# the existing convention. These are typically infra-level concerns.
PROD_ONLY = {"gunicorn", "sentry-sdk", "django-storages", "django-anymail"}


def parse_environment_yml(path):
    """Return (conda_deps, pip_deps) where each is a list of (name, version, section)."""
    conda = []
    pip = []
    current_section = None

    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            stripped = line.strip()

            section_match = re.match(r"# ── (.+?) ──", stripped)
            if section_match:
                current_section = section_match.group(1)
                continue

            if stripped.startswith("- pip:"):
                continue  # pip block header
            if current_section == "PyPI-only (fallback via pip)":
                if stripped.startswith("- ") and "==" in stripped:
                    name, ver = stripped[2:].split("==", 1)
                    pip.append((name.strip(), ver.strip(), current_section))
                continue

            if stripped.startswith("- ") and "=" in stripped and "==" not in stripped:
                # conda-style: - pkg=1.0
                entry = stripped[2:]
                if entry.startswith("pip"):
                    continue
                name, ver = entry.split("=", 1)
                conda.append((name.strip(), ver.strip(), current_section))

    return conda, pip


def format_pip_line(name, version, section):
    comment = f"  # {section}" if section else ""
    return f"{name}=={version}{comment}"


def write_requirements(packages, pip_deps, path, header_lines=None, include_line=None):
    lines = []
    if header_lines:
        lines.extend(header_lines)
    if include_line:
        lines.append(include_line)
        lines.append("")

    by_section = {}
    for pkg in packages:
        s = pkg[2] or "Other"
        by_section.setdefault(s, []).append(pkg)

    for section in sorted(by_section.keys()):
        sec_label = section.replace("_", " ").title()
        env_type = SECTION_CLASSIFICATION.get(section, "dev")
        lines.append(f"# ── {sec_label} ────────────────────────────────────────────")
        for name, ver, _ in sorted(by_section[section], key=lambda x: x[0].lower()):
            lines.append(format_pip_line(name, ver, section))
        lines.append("")

    # Append pip-only deps at the end
    if pip_deps:
        lines.append("# ── PyPI-only (not on conda-forge) ────────────────────────")
        for name, ver, section in sorted(pip_deps, key=lambda x: x[0].lower()):
            lines.append(format_pip_line(name, ver, section))
        lines.append("")

    existing = ""
    if os.path.exists(path):
        with open(path) as f:
            existing = f.read()

    new_content = "\n".join(lines) + "\n"
    if new_content != existing:
        with open(path, "w") as f:
            f.write(new_content)
        return True
    return False


def main():
    conda_deps, pip_deps = parse_environment_yml(ENV_YML)

    prod_pkgs = [d for d in conda_deps
                 if d[2] and SECTION_CLASSIFICATION.get(d[2]) == "prod"
                 and d[0] not in PROD_ONLY]
    prod_only_pkgs = [d for d in conda_deps
                      if d[0] in PROD_ONLY]
    dev_pkgs = [d for d in conda_deps
                if d[2] and SECTION_CLASSIFICATION.get(d[2]) == "dev"]

    base_prologue = [
        "# Generated from environment.yml — do not edit directly.",
        "# Run: python scripts/export_requirements.py",
        "",
    ]
    prod_prologue = [
        "# Generated from environment.yml — do not edit directly.",
        "# Production-only extras (added to base.txt).",
        "",
    ]
    local_prologue = [
        "# Generated from environment.yml — do not edit directly.",
        "# Full frozen environment (base + dev).",
        "",
    ]

    changed = []

    # ── base.txt — production dependencies ──
    base_path = os.path.join(REQS_DIR, "base.txt")
    if write_requirements(prod_pkgs, [], base_path, header_lines=base_prologue):
        changed.append("base.txt")

    # ── production.txt — production-only extras referencing base.txt ──
    prod_path = os.path.join(REQS_DIR, "production.txt")
    if write_requirements(
        prod_only_pkgs, pip_deps, prod_path,
        header_lines=prod_prologue,
        include_line="-r base.txt",
    ):
        changed.append("production.txt")

    # ── local.txt — full environment (includes all prod + dev + pip) ──
    local_path = os.path.join(REQS_DIR, "local.txt")
    if write_requirements(
        prod_pkgs + prod_only_pkgs + dev_pkgs, pip_deps, local_path,
        header_lines=local_prologue,
    ):
        changed.append("local.txt")

    # ── Report ──
    if not changed:
        print("✓ All requirements/*.txt are up to date with environment.yml.")
        return 0

    print(f"✓ Updated: {', '.join(changed)}")
    print(f"  Source:  environment.yml ({len(conda_deps)} conda + {len(pip_deps)} pip packages)")
    print(f"  base.txt:        {len(prod_pkgs)} production packages")
    print(f"  production.txt:  {len(prod_only_pkgs)} prod-only + {len(pip_deps)} pip-only")
    print(f"  local.txt:       {len(prod_pkgs) + len(prod_only_pkgs) + len(dev_pkgs)} total + {len(pip_deps)} pip-only")
    print("")
    print("  To install with conda:")
    print("    conda env create -f environment.yml")
    print("")
    print("  Or with pip (dev):")
    print("    pip install -r requirements/local.txt")
    print("")
    print("  Or with pip (production):")
    print("    pip install -r requirements/production.txt")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

**Current state:**
1. **Docker builds**: Two-stage pip wheel build. Stage 1 installs build deps + builds wheels via `pip wheel -r requirements/{local,production}.txt`. Stage 2 installs from those wheels with `--no-index`.
2. **CI (GitHub Actions)**:

If we switch to conda for the Python env, the fundamental question is: **where does conda run?** Three options:

**Option A: Docker images still use pip** (requirements.txt generated from environment.yml SSOT)

**Option B: Docker images switch to conda** (install conda in Docker, use environment.yml)
- Dockerfiles grow `miniconda` installation step
- Two-stage build changes: conda env export → pip install in run stage, or run-stage conda
- Larger images (conda runtime ~500MB added)
- CI: longer build times, bigger images
- Dependabot: cannot parse `environment.yml` natively

**Option C: Hybrid** — CI and local dev use conda + pip; Docker stays pip
- CI: add a conda-based job for linting/testing outside Docker
- Docker: unchanged (still uses pip wheel build from generated requirements/*.txt)
- Dependabot: watch `environment.yml` and `requirements/*.txt`
- Most practical approach

Let me articulate this clearly.

text:
Here's the full picture based on the current setup:

---

## Current Architecture

```
                           ┌─ requirements/base.txt ──┐
  environment.yml ──(new)──├─ requirements/production.txt │── Docker two-stage pip wheel build
  (SSOT)                   └─ requirements/local.txt ────┘
                              ↑
                        Dependabot watches these

  CI (GitHub Actions):
    Linter → actions/setup-python + pre-commit/action
    Tests  → docker compose build → docker compose run pytest
```

Three viable approaches, ordered by disruption:

---

## Option A: Docker Stays Pip, Conda Is for Local Dev Only (Recommended)

**Changes needed:**

| Layer | Change |
|---|---|
| **`scripts/export_requirements.py`** | Already written — runs in CI `--check` mode to prevent drift |
| **CI linter job** | Install conda → `conda env create -f environment.yml` → `conda run -n acers pre-commit run --all-files`. Optional: keep `actions/setup-python` for speed if pre-commit deps are light |
| **CI pytest job (Docker)** | **No change** — Docker still builds pip wheels from `requirements/local.txt` |
| **Dependabot** | Add `conda` ecosystem entry pointing at `environment.yml`; keep `pip` ecosystem for `requirements/*.txt` (Dependabot supports conda natively) |
| **Local dev** | `conda env create -f environment.yml` instead of `pip install -r requirements/local.txt`; Docker dev unchanged |
| **`.pre-commit-config.yaml`** | No change if pre-commit manages its own venv; add `conda run -n acers` wrapper if hooks need project packages |
| **Justfile** | Add `conda env create`, `conda env update`, `export-requirements` recipes |

**New CI job flow:**
```yaml
# linter (new conda path)
- uses: conda-incubator/setup-miniconda@v3
  with:
    environment-file: environment.yml
    activate-environment: acers
- run: conda run -n acers pre-commit run --all-files

# pytest (unchanged Docker path)
- run: docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml build django
- run: docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml run django pytest

# drift gate
- run: python scripts/export_requirements.py --check
```

**Downside:** Two environment definitions coexist — `environment.yml` is SSOT, but `requirements/*.txt` still drive Docker. The `--check` gate enforces sync, but a stale `requirements/*.txt` would only be caught at CI time.

---

## Option B: Docker Goes All-In on Conda

**Changes needed:**

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| **Both Dockerfiles** | Add `COPY environment.yml .` and `conda env create -f environment.yml` in build stage. This replaces the two-stage pip wheel pattern with a single conda environment |
| **`compose/local/django/Dockerfile`** | Install `miniforge`, copy `environment.yml`, run `conda env create`, activate in entrypoint |
| **`compose/production/django/Dockerfile`** | Same — but now the image embeds an entire conda env (~500 MB overhead from conda itself). Must use `conda run` or activate in the entrypoint script |
| **CI** | No pip wheel stage; `docker compose build django` does `conda env create` inside the container |
| **Dependabot** | Change `pip` ecosystem to `conda` pointing at `environment.yml` |
| **Local dev** | `conda env create -f environment.yml`, Docker images become larger |

**Example build-stage diff for `compose/local/django/Dockerfile`:**
```dockerfile
# Replace:
FROM python AS python-build-stage
COPY ./requirements .
RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /usr/src/app/wheels -r local.txt

# With:
FROM continuumio/miniconda3:latest AS conda-env
COPY environment.yml .
RUN conda env create -f environment.yml && \
    conda clean --all --yes

# Run stage installs conda env's site-packages into the slim image
# via pip freeze or a mount — complex and fragile.
```

**Problems:**
- conda envs are **immutable inside containers** — activation requires shell wrappers
- Image size balloons: conda runtime adds ~500 MB, and pre-linked C libraries duplicate what apt provides
- No official `slim` conda base image; you're on `continuumio/miniconda3` (Debian 11, 600 MB baseline) vs the current `python:3.12.8-slim-bookworm` (~120 MB)
- The two-stage wheel cache pattern breaks — every build re-resolves everything from conda
- `psycopg` v3 missing from conda-forge means the pip fallback reintroduces a pip dependency anyway

**Bottom line:** Not recommended for containerized deployments. Conda's value (SAT solver, pre-linked binaries) is wasted inside Docker where `pip wheel` + `--no-index` already guarantees deterministic builds, and the layered FS means C library linkage is already solved.

---

## Option C: Hybrid (Recommended Production Pattern)

Keep Docker on pip, but **run CI linting and tests natively via conda** to exercise the actual environment:

| Layer | Change |
|---|---|
| **CI linter** | `setup-miniconda` → `conda env create -f environment.yml` → `conda run -n acers pre-commit run --all-files` |
| **CI pytest** | Add a **parallel conda-native job** (no Docker): `setup-miniconda` → `conda env create -f environment.yml` → `DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///test.db conda run -n acers pytest`. Keeps the existing Docker job as the production-fidelity gate |
| **CI drift gate** | `python scripts/export_requirements.py --check` after every env.yml change |
| **Docker** | No change — still builds pip wheels from `requirements/*.txt` |
| **Dependabot** | Add `conda` ecosystem for `environment.yml`; keep `pip` for `requirements/*.txt` |
| **Local dev** | `conda env create -f environment.yml` for local Python work; `docker compose up` unchanged for full-stack testing |
| **`.devcontainer/`** | If devcontainer exists (it does), add conda installation and `environment.yml` to the devcontainer `postCreateCommand` |

**New CI jobs:**
```yaml
linter:
  steps:
    - uses: conda-incubator/setup-miniconda@v3
      with:
        environment-file: environment.yml
        activate-environment: acers
    - run: conda run -n acers pre-commit run --all-files

pytest-conda:  # fast feedback — exercises the conda dependency tree
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: conda-incubator/setup-miniconda@v3
      with:
        environment-file: environment.yml
        activate-environment: acers
    - run: conda run -n acers pytest

pytest-docker:  # production fidelity — runs inside actual Docker stack
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - run: docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml build django
    - run: docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml run django pytest

check-requirements-sync:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
    - run: python scripts/export_requirements.py --check
```

---

## Summary Comparison

| Concern | Current (pip-only) | Option A (conda local + pip Docker) | Option B (conda everywhere) | Option C (conda CI + pip Docker) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Docker image size** | ~320 MB (slim) | unchanged | ~1.1 GB (+250%) | unchanged |
| **Docker build time** | ~2 min (cached wheels) | unchanged | ~5 min (no wheel cache) | unchanged |
| **CI lint speed** | ~30s setup-python | ~90s (conda solve) | ~90s | ~90s |
| **CI test isolation** | Full Docker stack | Full Docker stack | Full Docker stack | Both conda-native + Docker |
| **Dependabot** | pip ecosystem | pip + conda ecosystems | conda ecosystem | pip + conda ecosystems |
| **Local dev startup** | pip install -r | conda env create | conda env create | conda env create |
| **SSOT enforcement** | manual | `--check` gate | `environment.yml` is the only source | `--check` gate |
| **Risk** | None (current) | `requirements/*.txt` could drift from `environment.yml` | conda runtime bugs in Docker | Low — CI `--check` catches drift |
| **psycopg v3 migration** | `pip install psycopg[c]` | pip fallback in conda | blocked (not on conda-forge) | pip fallback in conda |

**My recommendation: Option C.** It gives you the fastest feedback loop (conda-native CI catches solve failures before Docker builds) while keeping zero changes to the production Docker images. The `--check` gate guarantees `requirements/*.txt` never drifts from `environment.yml`, so Docker continues building identically. The only incremental cost is adding `setup-miniconda` to CI (~60s per job) and one Dependabot config entry.
